chmmc-2013-power-01a.title: Read the expression
chmmc-2013-power-01a.body:
$0^*$ is any number of zeros, then a single $1$, then any number of zeros. So the strings are those with exactly one $1$ (and any number of $0$s before and after it).

**Answer: strings with exactly one 1**

chmmc-2013-power-01b.title: Read the expression
chmmc-2013-power-01b.body:
$\Sigma\Sigma$ is the set of strings of length $2$, and $(\Sigma\Sigma)^*$ is any number of them concatenated: exactly the strings of even length, including the empty string.

**Answer: strings of even length**

chmmc-2013-power-01c.title: Read the expression
chmmc-2013-power-01c.body:
The expression builds a string from optional $1$s, then repeated units $000$ each followed by any number of $1$s. Zeros therefore come in groups of exactly three, and two groups may touch (when $1^*$ is empty), so a maximal block of zeros has length $3,6,9,\dots$. Conversely any such string is generated (read it left to right: a block of $1$s, then each $000$ with the $1$s that follow it).

**Answer: every block of 0s has length a multiple of 3**

chmmc-2013-power-02a.title: Mark a $1$
chmmc-2013-power-02a.body:
A string has a $1$ iff it can be written as (anything) $1$ (anything): $\Sigma^*1\Sigma^*$.

**Answer: $\Sigma^*1\Sigma^*$**

chmmc-2013-power-02b.title: Split by the first symbol
chmmc-2013-power-02b.body:
If $w$ begins and ends with $0$, then either $w=0$ or $w=0u0$ with $u\in\Sigma^*$; similarly for $1$. So the language is $0\cup1\cup0\Sigma^*0\cup1\Sigma^*1$. (The official answer $0\Sigma^*0\cup1\Sigma^*1$ omits the one-symbol strings $0$ and $1$; if you treat a one-symbol string as having a different first and last symbol, that answer is also fine.)

**Answer: $0\cup1\cup0\Sigma^*0\cup1\Sigma^*1$**

chmmc-2013-power-02c.title: Count the 1s after the first symbol
chmmc-2013-power-02c.body:
The condition says the number of $1$s after the first symbol is even. After the first symbol $\Sigma$, the rest of the string consists of $0$s and $1$s with an even number of $1$s. Such a string is a concatenation of units that are either a single $0$ or a pair of $1$s with only $0$s between them ($10^*1$). So the answer is $\Sigma(0\cup10^*1)^*$, which is equivalent to $\Sigma0^*(10^*10^*)^*$. (The official $\Sigma(0^*10^*10^*)^*$ does not allow strings like $00$.)

**Answer: $\Sigma(0\cup10^*1)^*$**

chmmc-2013-power-03a.title: Geometric series
chmmc-2013-power-03a.body: $\sum a_nx^n=1+3x^2+9x^4+27x^6+\cdots=\sum_{n\ge0}(3x^2)^n$, a geometric series with first term $1$ and ratio $3x^2$. Since $(1-3x^2)\sum_{n}(3x^2)^n=1$ as formal power series (the sum telescopes), the closed form is $\dfrac1{1-3x^2}$. ∎

chmmc-2013-power-03b.title: Collect the coefficient of $x^n$
chmmc-2013-power-03b.body: Multiplying out, each term $a_kx^k\cdot b_mx^m$ contributes to $x^{k+m}$. The terms giving $x^n$ are exactly those with $k+m=n$, i.e. $m=n-k$ for $k=0,1,\dots,n$. Hence $c_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kb_{n-k}$. ∎

chmmc-2013-power-03c.title: Expand the four factors
chmmc-2013-power-03c.body: $\frac1{1-x^c}=1+x^c+x^{2c}+\cdots=\sum_{m\ge0}x^{cm}$. Multiplying the four series for $c=1,5,10,25$, a term of the product is $x^{p}\cdot x^{5u}\cdot x^{10v}\cdot x^{25w}$, obtained by choosing one term from each factor, with $p,u,v,w\ge0$ arbitrary. Each choice corresponds to using $p$ pennies, $u$ nickels, $v$ dimes and $w$ quarters, and has exponent $p+5u+10v+25w$, the total value in cents. So the coefficient of $x^n$ is the number of quadruples $(p,u,v,w)$ of non-negative integers with $p+5u+10v+25w=n$, which is exactly $A_n$. (Equivalently, applying the product formula of 3b repeatedly.) ∎

chmmc-2013-power-04a.title: Shift and subtract
chmmc-2013-power-04a.body: Let $f(x)=\sum F_nx^n$. Then $xf(x)=\sum F_{n-1}x^n$ and $x^2f(x)=\sum F_{n-2}x^n$. In $f-xf-x^2f$ the coefficient of $x^n$ for $n\ge2$ is $F_n-F_{n-1}-F_{n-2}=0$; the constant term is $F_0=1$ and the $x$ term is $F_1-F_0=0$. Hence $(1-x-x^2)f(x)=1$ and $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1-x-x^2}$. ∎

chmmc-2013-power-04b.title: Clear the denominator
chmmc-2013-power-04b.body: Multiplying, $(1+2x-x^3)\sum a_nx^n=1+x^2$. The coefficient of $x^n$ on the left is $a_n+2a_{n-1}-a_{n-3}$ (with $a_{m}=0$ for $m<0$), and on the right it is $0$ for $n\ge3$. Hence $a_n+2a_{n-1}-a_{n-3}=0$ for $n\ge3$. ∎

chmmc-2013-power-04c.title: Compare coefficients
chmmc-2013-power-04c.body: Clearing the denominator, $\left(\sum_n a_nx^n\right)(c_0+c_1x+\cdots+c_kx^k)=p(x)$. The coefficient of $x^n$ on the left is $\sum_{j=0}^{k}c_ja_{n-j}$ (with $a_m=0$ for $m<0$; for $n\ge k$ all indices are non-negative). The right side $p(x)$ has degree $d$, so its coefficient of $x^n$ is $0$ for $n>d$. Therefore $c_0a_n+c_1a_{n-1}+\cdots+c_ka_{n-k}=0$ for $n>d$, $n\ge k$. ∎

chmmc-2013-power-05.title: Split by length
chmmc-2013-power-05.body: Let $a_k$ and $b_k$ be the numbers of strings of length $k$ in $A$ and $B$. A string of length $n$ in $A\circ B$ is $xy$ with $x\in A$ of some length $k$ and $y\in B$ of length $n-k$, $0\le k\le n$, and (by the unique-splitting assumption) each such string comes from exactly one pair $(x,y)$. So the number of such strings is $c_n=\sum_{k=0}^na_kb_{n-k}$, which by problem 3(b) is the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f_A(x)f_B(x)$. ∎

chmmc-2013-power-06.title: Disjoint union
chmmc-2013-power-06.body: Because $A$ and $B$ share no strings, the number of strings of length $n$ in $A\cup B$ is $a_n+b_n$. So the coefficient of $x^n$ is $a_n+b_n$, i.e. $f_{A\cup B}=f_A+f_B$. ∎

chmmc-2013-power-07.title: Sum over the number of factors
chmmc-2013-power-07.body: $A^*=A^0\cup A^1\cup A^2\cup\cdots$ with $A^0=\{\varepsilon\}$ (generating function $1$). By problem 5 and induction, $A^k$ has generating function $f_A(x)^k$ (since $A^{k+1}=A^k\circ A$). The sets $A^k$ are pairwise disjoint (by the unique-splitting assumption and $\varepsilon\notin A$, strings in $A^k$ are built from exactly $k$ nonempty pieces), so by problem 6 the generating function of $A^*$ is $$1+f_A+f_A^2+\cdots=\frac{1}{1-f_A(x)}.$$ ∎

chmmc-2013-power-08.title: Read it piece by piece
chmmc-2013-power-08.body:
$(00)^*0$ is an odd number of zeros, and $1\cup11$ is a block of one or two ones. The middle part $\big((00)^*0(1\cup11)\big)^*$ is a sequence of units 'odd block of $0$s followed by a block of one or two $1$s'. The prefix $\varepsilon\cup1\cup11$ allows an initial block of $1$s of size $1$ or $2$ (or none), and the suffix $\varepsilon\cup(00)^*0$ allows a final odd block of $0$s. Together: strings whose maximal $0$-blocks all have odd length and whose maximal $1$-blocks all have length $1$ or $2$. (A brute-force check of strings up to length 14 confirms this.)

**Answer: all $0$-blocks odd, all $1$-blocks of size 1 or 2**

chmmc-2013-power-09.title: Apply rules 5-7
chmmc-2013-power-09.body:
The generating functions are: $(00)^*0$: $\frac{x}{1-x^2}$; $1\cup11$: $x+x^2$; $\varepsilon\cup1\cup11$: $1+x+x^2$; $\varepsilon\cup(00)^*0$: $1+\frac{x}{1-x^2}$. The starred middle unit has generating function $\dfrac{x(x+x^2)}{1-x^2}$, so its star gives $\dfrac{1}{1-\frac{x^2+x^3}{1-x^2}}=\dfrac{1-x^2}{1-2x^2-x^3}$. Multiply: $$(1+x+x^2)\cdot\frac{1-x^2}{1-2x^2-x^3}\cdot\frac{1+x-x^2}{1-x^2}=\frac{(1+x+x^2)(1+x-x^2)}{1-2x^2-x^3}=\frac{1+2x+x^2-x^4}{1-2x^2-x^3}.$$ Its expansion $1+2x+3x^2+5x^3+7x^4+13x^5+19x^6+\cdots$ agrees with a direct count of the strings of each length.

**Answer: $\dfrac{1+2x+x^2-x^4}{1-2x^2-x^3}$**

chmmc-2013-power-10.title: From the generating function
chmmc-2013-power-10.body:
By problem 9, $f(x)=\dfrac{1+2x+x^2-x^4}{1-2x^2-x^3}$, so $(1-2x^2-x^3)f(x)=1+2x+x^2-x^4$. By problem 4(c) (numerator of degree $4$), comparing coefficients of $x^n$ for $n\ge5$ gives $a_n-2a_{n-2}-a_{n-3}=0$. Check with the counts $a_0,a_1,\dots=1,2,3,5,7,13,19,33,\dots$: $a_5=2a_3+a_2=10+3=13$, $a_6=2a_4+a_3=14+5=19$, $a_7=2\cdot13+7=33$. ✓

**Answer: $a_n=2a_{n-2}+a_{n-3}$**
